title: Apple releases firmware 9B47 for all AirPods with H2 chip
content:
Macworld





If you have any AirPods with an H2 chip, it’s time for an update. Apple has released firmware version 9B47 for all AirPods that use the H2. That includes:
AirPods Pro 2
AirPods Pro 3
AirPods 4
AirPods 5
AirPods Max 2
The previous firmware was 9A348 which added support from Custom EQ and GymKit. A version 9A350 was released just for the AirPods 5, to bring them up to date with those features.
Apple has not yet disclosed the contents of this release on its AirPods Firmware page. It’s likely this is just “bug fixes and performance improvements,” as there aren’t any new iOS or macOS features that should require new firmware.
You can’t update your AirPods firmware manually. But there are steps you can take to check your firmware version and make sure that Apple updates your AirPods sooner rather than later.
How to update AirPods on iPhone, iPad, or Mac
Make sure that your AirPods are in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac. Make sure that device is connected to Wi-Fi.
Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid.
Plug in the charging case (plug the USB cable into a power adapter and the charging case).
Keep the lid of the charging case closed.
Wait at least 30 minutes.
Open the lid of the charging case to reconnect your AirPods to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.
Check the firmware version again.
How to check the firmware version of your AirPods
On iPhone or iPad: With your AirPods nearby and the case open, open Settings on your iPhone or iPad. You’ll see your AirPods listed at the top of Settings. Tap that, and scroll down to the bottom of your AirPods settings to see the Version.
On Mac: Open System Settings. Select Bluetooth, then click the (i) next to your connected AirPods. The Version will be listed there, along with other information.

title: iFixit's PROLED MacBook Pro Teardown Reveals Logo LEDs
content:
iFixit today took apart Apple's touchscreen PROLED MacBook Pro to see how Apple shed weight, what powers the logo, and how it compares to the 14-inch M6 ‌MacBook Pro‌.



Apple added a glowing logo on the back of the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌, but since there's no backlight to illuminate it, Apple used four LEDs, a reflective layer, and a diffuser to create an even glow. When the light is off, the logo's two-way mirror coating gives it a shiny finish.

OLED.

Apple says the PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌ has a hinge designed for touch, but iFixit said it's basically identical to the M6 ‌MacBook Pro‌'s hinge, just stiffer, so it better holds its angle when the display is tapped at the top.

The Thunderbolt/USB-C ports and fans are replaceable, but the logic board has to come out. The HDMI port and SDXC card slot are soldered to the logic board, so they're not as easily replaced. The SSD and memory are also soldered.

Touch ID. iFixit said the touchscreen didn't add any new parts pairing problems.

The PROLED ‌MacBook Pro‌'s trackpad is a little bit smaller than the M6 model's, and weight was shed by removing some aluminum from the lower chassis. The lower case weighs 364 grams vs. 456 grams for the M6 model. The display assembly is 101 grams lighter despite the touchscreen and the glowing Apple logo, and the battery is two grams lighter too.

Magic Keyboard with Touch ID & Numeric Pad: (RRP £179)

Does Apple have sales?
Apple rarely discounts its own products. Even during its annual Black Friday shopping event, which runs from Black Friday to Cyber Monday, Apple typically offers gift cards with eligible purchases instead of cutting prices.
That doesn’t mean you have to pay full price. Third-party retailers such as Amazon, Best Buy and other Apple resellers regularly discount Apple products throughout the year.
Some of the best savings on Apple products come during Amazon’s Prime Day events. We saw substantial discounts during Prime Day in June 2026, and another Amazon Prime Day sale takes place on October 6 and 7, when we expect to see more deals on Macs, iPads, AirPods and other Apple devices.
Apple also offers year-round education discounts to students, teachers and education staff. During its annual Back To School promotion – usually running for around three months from June or July in many countries (and from January in Australia, New Zealand and other Southern Hemisphere markets) – eligible higher education students can receive a free pair of AirPods or an Apple Pencil with selected Mac and iPad purchases.
Finally, don’t overlook the Apple Certified Refurbished Store, where you can buy refurbished Macs, iPads and other Apple products at a discount. These devices are thoroughly tested, include a new battery and outer casing where applicable, and come with the same one-year warranty as new Apple products. Following Apple’s June 2026 price increases, some refurbished models can be particularly attractive because their prices haven’t risen in the same way as equivalent new models.
 FAQ 


1.
When are the best Apple deals? 
Apple deals are generally best during major retail events like Black Friday and Amazon Prime Day, or specifically for students during Apple’s annual “Back to School” promotion. While Apple itself rarely offers direct price cuts on new hardware, third-party resellers frequently discount products throughout the year.
The optimal time to buy depends heavily on the product’s release cycle and the specific retailer, though: 
iPhones: The best time to buy is often in the spring or summer, several months after the September launch, when third-party resellers begin offering deeper discounts . Conversely, the worst time is August, just before new models arrive and trigger price drops on older generations.
Macs and iPads: These see significant discounts during Black Friday (late November) and Amazon Prime Day (typically July and October). For students, the Back to School event (running June–September in the U.S. and July–October in the U.K.) is ideal, as Apple often bundles free accessories like AirPods or Apple Pencils with purchases.
Apple Watch: Major savings are typically found during Black Friday and Prime Day events.





2.
Are Apple refurbished deals worth it?
Apple refurbished deals are widely considered worth it, particularly when purchasing directly from the official Apple Refurbished Store, where products are restored to a “like-new” condition. While third-party resellers often provide steeper discounts, Apple’s own process is uniquely rigorous, offering a balance of significant savings and the same protections as a brand-new purchase. 
Buying directly from Apple is often described as “almost indistinguishable” from buying new. According to our guide How much can you save at Apple’s Refurbished Store?, the company puts every device through a “stringent refurbishment process” that includes full functional testing, thorough cleaning, and inspection.
Key benefits of the official Apple Refurbished Store include:
Hardware Replacements: Refurbished iPads and iPhones receive a brand-new battery and outer shell .
Warranty and Support: All products come with a standard one-year limited warranty, 90 days of technical support, and are eligible for AppleCare .
Full Accessories: Devices are repackaged in a plain white box with all original manuals and cables .
Savings: You can typically save around 15% off the retail price for recent models, with much higher discounts on older generations.
Avoid the Apple price hikes: Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store sells products at the old, pre-hike prices – meaning you can effectively sidestep the recent price increases entirely. 





3.
Is it better to buy Apple products from Amazon or Apple?
Deciding whether to buy Apple products from Amazon or directly from Apple depends on whether you prioritize immediate cost savings or the specific perks and guarantees offered by the manufacturer. While Amazon often provides deeper discounts, Apple offers unique benefits like trade-in credits, education pricing, and the assurance of receiving the latest models.





4.
Does Apple ever discount products directly?
Apple rarely provides direct price reductions on its new products, preferring to maintain steady Old MSRP pricing throughout a product’s lifecycle. Instead of traditional discounts, the company typically utilizes alternative methods to provide value directly to consumers, such as gift card incentives during major shopping events, education pricing, and a dedicated refurbished store. 
While you will not often see a lower price tag on a new iPhone or Mac at the Apple Store, the company does offer several ways to save:
Apple Shopping Events: During events like Black Friday and Cyber Monday, Apple typically offers gift cards rather than price cuts. For example, in the 2025 holiday season, Apple provided gift cards ranging from $25 to $250 for eligible purchases.
Education Store: Students, teachers, and higher education staff can access year-round discounts on Macs and iPads . During the annual “Back to School” event, Apple often includes a “freebie” like AirPods or an Apple Pencil with qualifying purchases.
Apple Refurbished Store: This is the primary way to get a direct price reduction from Apple. Products are fully reconditioned, come with a one-year warranty, and can be discounted by hundreds of dollars or pounds.
Trade-In Program: Apple allows customers to trade in old devices to receive credit toward a new purchase, effectively lowering the out-of-pocket cost.

title: Best Apple Watch Black Friday deals: Savings on Series 12, 11, SE, and Ultra
content:
Macworld






Best Black Friday Apple Watch deals so far: U.S.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: $699.99 ($99 off, MSRP $799) – already the best price we’ve seen




Best Black Friday Apple Watch deals so far: U.K.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: £729 (£20 off, RRP £749) – the best price we’ve seen so far
Apple Watch Ultra 3: £519 (£230 less than Apple Watch Ultra 4) – the best price we’ve seen




PRICES CHECKED 10 NOVEMBER, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is a great time to buy an Apple Watch, with retailers discounting everything from the affordable SE to the premium Ultra. Last year’s U.S. offers included $50 off the SE 3, up to $70 off the then-new Series 11, and $100 off the Ultra 3. Older models brought bigger savings, including $150 off the Series 10 and $200 off the Ultra 2. In the U.K., clearance offers were particularly attractive: the Series 10 was up to £130 off at Currys, while Argos cut £200 from the Ultra 2’s original price.
October Prime Day brought discounts on this year’s models, too. In the U.S., the 42mm Series 12 fell to $349, the 40mm SE 3 to $199, and the Ultra 4 to $774 – savings of $50, $50, and $25 respectively. U.K. highlights included the SE 3 at £199 and the previous-generation Series 11 at £259.
This Black Friday, we’d watch the Series 12 for discounts on our best Apple Watch for most people, the SE 3 for an affordable entry point, and the Ultra 4 for longer battery life and outdoor features. Remaining Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock could offer particularly good value if priced sufficiently below their replacements. Below, we explain which offers are worth taking and when to wait; for savings across Apple’s other products, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Which Apple Watch should you buy this Black Friday?


Apple Watch Series 12 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Series 12 is the Apple Watch we recommend for most people. It combines Apple’s new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate measurements, a Readiness score, and a tougher display with up to 24 hours of battery life.
A worthwhile Black Friday discount could make it an attractive purchase, but compare it with remaining Series 11 stock. The older model has the same quoted battery life, so a substantial saving may outweigh the newer health features.
U.S. Black Friday price: During October Prime Day, the 42mm GPS Series 12 fell to $349, while the 46mm version reached $399 – $50 off each. Last Black Friday, its predecessor, the Series 11, received discounts of up to $70. So far this Black Friday month we’ve seen prices drop by $9, but we expect they will drop further.
U.K. Black Friday price: We didn’t see Series 12 discounts during October Prime Day and so far this November there have been no price drops, but we are hopeful.  


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 4 – Best for battery life and outdoor adventures

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Ultra 4 is our choice for endurance athletes, outdoor enthusiasts, and buyers who prioritize battery life. It offers up to 50 hours of normal use, satellite communication, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and Apple’s new Health Sensing System.
It’s more watch than most people need, but the current $699.99 offer is substantially below October Prime Day’s $774 price, making it worth considering if you want the latest Ultra. Compare it with the Ultra 3, though, which retains many of its outdoor features but has a shorter 42-hour battery-life rating.
U.S. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the Ultra 4 down to $774, a $25 saving. This November we’ve already seen the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for $699.99 on Amazon: that’s $99 off. 
U.K. Black Friday price: The Ultra 4 remained at its full £749 price during October Prime Day, but we’ve already seen it drop by £20 to £729 at Amazon. 


						

							


Apple Watch SE 3 – Our best budget choice

				
					

				
			
Apple / Amazon




The SE 3 is the best-value option for buyers who want the core Apple Watch experience. It includes an always-on display, temperature sensing, fast charging, and the S10 chip, but lacks ECG, blood oxygen monitoring, and the newer Health Sensing System.
It remains part of Apple’s current lineup despite launching in 2025. A strong Black Friday offer could make it an excellent affordable purchase, although its previous discounts mean there’s little reason to settle for a token reduction.
U.S. Black Friday price: Both last Black Friday and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to $199 and the 44mm version to $229 – $50 below their regular prices. So far, the U.S. price drop is just $9 at Amazon, so we’d hold out for bigger savings.
U.K. Black Friday price: Black Friday 2025 and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to £199 and the 44mm version to £229, saving £20. So far we haven’t seen any price drops for Black Friday 2026.


						

							


Apple Watch Ultra 3 – Best clearance option for outdoor enthusiasts

				
					

				
			
Apple




The Ultra 3 is worth considering if you want a rugged Apple Watch without paying for the latest model. It offers satellite communication, dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and up to 42 hours of battery life.
You give up the Ultra 4’s longer battery life and newer Health Sensing System. Compare their actual selling prices: the Ultra 3 needs to be sufficiently cheaper to justify choosing the older generation.
U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the Ultra 3 fell to $699, a $100 saving. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models, so it didn’t identify a comparable new-stock offer. So far this November we’ve seen the Apple Watch Ultra 3 for $649, but that’s only $51 cheaper than the Ultra 4, so we’d favor the newer model.  
U.K. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the Ultra 3 was £719, or £30 off. October Prime Day listed it at £569. The price is even lower this November – you can get it for £519 at Amazon, £230 less than the usual Apple Watch Ultra 4 price. 


						

							


Apple Watch Series 11 – Best clearance option for everyday use

				
					

				
			
Apple Watch Series 11




The Series 11 could be a better-value everyday watch than the Series 12 if the price gap is large enough. It has the same quoted 24-hour battery life, although it misses the newer Health Sensing System and Audio Intelligence features.
For buyers who don’t need those additions, a substantial clearance discount could be more useful than a small saving on the latest model.
U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the 42mm GPS Series 11 reached $339, while the 46mm version was $359 – savings of $60 and $70, respectively. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models in the U.S. and so far that’s all we are seeing this November.
U.K. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the 42mm Series 11 to £259 and the 46mm version to £299. Last Black Friday’s bigger clearance offers were on the preceding Series 10, which was available for £279 in 42mm and £299 in 46mm. In November 2026 you can get a Series 11 for £299, £120 less than the equivalent Series 12.


						

							







Should you buy an Apple Watch now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an Apple Watch immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer matches or comes close to a previous low for the same model and configuration, it can be worth taking – particularly if you want a specific size, color, or band combination.
October Prime Day prices provide useful benchmarks. In the U.S., the Series 12 fell to $349 for the 42mm GPS model and $399 for the 46mm version, while the Ultra 4 reached $774. The SE 3 was $199 in 40mm and $229 in 44mm. Those SE prices also appeared last Black Friday, so we’d look for offers matching or beating them. In the U.K., October highlights included the 40mm SE 3 at £199 and the older 42mm Series 11 at £259.
The Series 12 and Ultra 4 only arrived in September, so finding a better price is the main reason to wait. If you don’t need a watch immediately, those previous offers give you a useful starting point for deciding whether to buy now or hold out.
Compare retailers, too. Last Black Friday, Walmart offered $150 off the Series 10, while U.K. shoppers could find up to £130 off at Currys and £200 off the Ultra 2’s original price at Argos. Our guide to the best time to buy an Apple Watch has more advice on choosing when to purchase.


						

							


Should you buy an older Apple Watch?

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent purchases if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4. Both retain many of their replacements’ core features, although you miss the newer Health Sensing System and, with the Ultra 3, the Ultra 4’s longer battery life.
Compare actual selling prices, matching case size, material, connectivity, and band where possible. A $50 difference between a Series 11 and Series 12 may not be enough to justify giving up the newer model’s health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation. A discounted Series 11 could also be worth considering alongside the SE 3 if a small premium gets you features you’ll use.
Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2, and original Ultra: those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with the latest software, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra and the SE 3 is the only supported SE. Missing the latest software doesn’t make an older watch unusable, but it makes it harder to recommend as a purchase today.
The Series 9, Series 10, and Ultra 2 can still be worth considering at sufficiently low prices. However, compatibility with today’s software doesn’t guarantee how many future upgrades they’ll receive. Weigh the savings against the watch’s age and features, rather than assuming every supported generation offers equally good value.


						

							


Apple Watch deals to avoid 

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t let a bigger advertised discount tempt you into paying more for a cellular Apple Watch you won’t use. If your iPhone is usually nearby, a GPS model can already handle calls, messages, and notifications through your phone. It can also track runs, use Apple Pay, and play downloaded music without your iPhone. As our experience testing a cellular Apple Watch showed, the extra connectivity may add little to everyday use.
Cellular is worth considering if you regularly leave your iPhone behind and want to remain contactable without Wi-Fi, or you’re setting up a watch for a child without an iPhone. Otherwise, you could pay extra for the hardware and then add an ongoing mobile-plan charge for a feature you rarely need. You don’t have to activate a plan on a cellular model, so it can still be a good buy if its sale price matches or beats the GPS version. Our GPS versus cellular Apple Watch guide explains the trade-offs.
Check the rest of the configuration, too. A premium case material or expensive band can make a heavily discounted watch cost more than a simpler version that meets your needs. Judge offers against previous selling prices as well as the advertised reduction: a large saving from the original launch price doesn’t necessarily mean exceptional value. Check any spending requirements, contracts, trade-ins, or rebates attached to offers advertising a “free” Apple Watch.
Finally, check whether you’re buying a new, refurbished, or used watch, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For a used or refurbished model, check the stated battery condition and confirm that it has been removed from the previous owner’s account and Activation Lock. Make sure the watch is compatible with your iPhone before ordering.


						

							


How we choose Apple Watch deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on Apple Watch reviews and everyday wear. We consider comfort, performance, battery life, charging, health and fitness features, and value – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our Series 12 review assessed battery life and charging performance alongside its newer health features. We also draw on everyday experience: our cellular Apple Watch testing examines whether staying connected without an iPhone justified the extra hardware and subscription costs.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. We check the generation, case size, material, connectivity, and included band so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside discounted replacements.
Our Best Apple Watch guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the right choice: your budget, wrist size, activities, and the features you need all matter.

title: iPad Mini 2021 vs. 2026 Buyer's Guide: Is It Worth Upgrading?
content:
Apple's eighth-generation iPad mini went on sale earlier this month with a larger OLED display, a thinner and lighter design, the A20 Pro chip, and water and dust resistance. If you still use the sixth-generation ‌iPad mini‌ from 2021, the upgrade also brings changes that debuted on the 2024 model, including Apple Intelligence, Apple Pencil Pro support, and twice the USB-C transfer speed.


The new ‌iPad mini‌ starts at $699 for 128GB with Wi-Fi or $849 with cellular in the United States. The discontinued 2021 model started at $499 and $649, respectively, with 64GB of storage. Both support iPadOS 27.2, have Touch ID in the top button, and are rated for up to 10 hours of web browsing over Wi-Fi or watching video. Both displays also run at 60Hz.

Starts at $699 (Wi-Fi) or $849 (Wi-Fi + Cellular)




Both the 2021 and 2026 models are rated for up to nine hours of web browsing over cellular. Apple claims up to 50% faster cellular data speeds with the C2 modem compared with the 2024 ‌iPad mini‌.

Should You Upgrade?

If your 2021 model still feels responsive and lasts long enough for reading, browsing, and taking notes, keeping it makes sense for now, and if battery life is your only complaint, a battery service may be enough.

However, for many 2021 ‌iPad mini‌ owners, the 2026 model is a worthwhile upgrade. If you've had yours since launch, its battery has had five years to wear down, and 64GB can feel cramped if you keep games or downloaded video on it. The new model gives you a fresh battery and twice the storage if you're coming from the 64GB version. Apple still rates both models for up to 10 hours when new, but the 2026 model can charge to 50% in around 30 minutes with a 35W or higher adapter.

The ‌OLED‌ display and lighter design are the changes you're most likely to notice every day. The screen can get dimmer for reading in bed and brighter for HDR video, and the lower weight makes the ‌iPad mini‌ easier to hold one-handed for long stretches. Both displays run at 60Hz, with no ProMotion. The A20 Pro and extra memory matter more if you play demanding games, edit photos or video, or often find that apps reload when you switch back to them.

iPad is propped up horizontally, and extended display support lets you use a monitor as a separate workspace.

Which Model Should You Buy?

The discontinued 2024 iPad mini is a good middle ground if your 2021 model is showing its age and you're happy with its display. It gives you more base storage, ‌Apple Intelligence‌, faster USB-C transfers, and ‌Apple Pencil‌ Pro support, and you can reuse your existing Smart Folio. Apple lists the 128GB Wi-Fi model for $509 through its Certified Refurbished store when available, with a new battery and a one-year warranty. Remaining new stock from third-party retailers is also worth considering at a low enough price.

If prices are close at the same storage capacity, buy the 2026 model. At $699, it makes the most sense if you specifically want the ‌OLED‌ display, lighter body, or water resistance. If you use a Smart Folio, factor in $79 for the redesigned version. The USB-C ‌Apple Pencil‌ works with either newer model, while the second-generation ‌Apple Pencil‌ needs replacing. Both newer cellular models use eSIM, so check with your carrier if you currently use a physical SIM.

A used 2021 ‌iPad mini‌ is still a reasonable buy at around $300 or lower if you want a second device for reading, notes, or streaming and 64GB is enough. Battery condition matters more than cosmetic wear; if the price of a 256GB unit or the cost of a battery service brings it close to a refurbished 2024 model, the newer device is still the better buy.

title: New Apple TV Sign Language Feature Announced
content:
Apple today announced a new accessibility feature for the Apple TV app that gives viewers the option to watch supported movies and shows with on-screen sign language interpretation. An interpreter will appear in the bottom-right corner of the screen, with the experience said to have been designed and tested by Deaf and native signers.


The feature is available in the Apple TV app on devices running iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, and visionOS 27.2 or later.

Being Heumann, which chronicles the story of disability rights activist Judy Heumann. The movie begins streaming in the Apple TV app on Friday. 

F1, and for the movies Way of the Warrior Kid and Greyhound later this year. Over time, the option will expand to additional Apple Original films and series.

"Each performance is carefully crafted to fit and complement the Apple Original film it interprets," said Apple.

Titles with sign language interpretation will be labeled with a Sign Language icon. Viewers can enable the feature in the Apple TV app's settings, and then press the Sign Language button while watching a supported movie or show. Search will also make it easier to find titles that feature sign language with simple phrases like "with ASL."


As sign language interpretation becomes more widely available across streaming services, a new "Movies & Shows with American Sign Language" collection will be added to the Apple TV app. Apple mentioning plural "streaming services" suggests that the option will eventually be available for more than just Apple Originals.

title: Disable Touch on MacBook Pro PROLED XDR and When Using Sidecar
content:
Apple has long rejected the idea of a touchscreen Mac, so moving ahead with one was always going to be a major shift in the company's thinking. In 2010, Steve Jobs argued that "touch surfaces don't want to be vertical," citing the arm fatigue that comes from repeatedly reaching up to a screen.

Some would call this sacrilege...

More than a decade later, in 2021, Apple's then-hardware engineering chief John Ternus remarked that the Mac was made exclusively for indirect input and that Apple saw no compelling reason to change its approach.

interview with Joanna Stern.

Touch Comes to the Mac

Fast forward to 2026, and Apple has had a change of heart. The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is the first Mac to adopt touchscreen technology. Many younger people who grew up with smartphones and tablets expect to interact with their computers the same way they do with their mobile devices, and that expectation appears to have twisted Apple's arm (no pun intended).

Of course, just because the new MacBook Pro models have a touchscreen doesn't mean you have to use it. If you forget it's even there, you can turn off the function and pretend it doesn't exist. If you use Sidecar with an iPad on another Mac, you can turn off touch in the same way.

Turn Off Touch on MacBook Pro and Sidecar

The steps are the same whether you want to disable the MacBook Pro's touchscreen or touch input in Sidecar:

Click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of the menu bar and choose System Settings....

Select Accessibility in the sidebar.

Under "Physical and Motor," click Touch.

Toggle on the switch next to Ignore Touch Gestures.

That's all there is to it. Your Mac will now ignore touch input, and since the setting covers Sidecar too, an iPad you use as a second display will ignore touches as well. If you ever want touch back, return to the same screen and toggle off Ignore Touch Gestures.

Touch Friendly, Not Touch First

If some gestures prove useful but others keep being triggered by accident, you can adjust them individually instead of disabling touch altogether. In System Settings, select Touch Display in the sidebar, where each gesture can be switched off, and Swipe between spaces, Mission Control, and App Exposé also have pop-up menus for changing how the gesture is performed. 


Don't overlook the fact that the Accessibility ➝ Touch screen (where "Ignore Touch Gestures" lives) offers further customization options. Touch Accommodations changes how the screen responds to taps, swipes, and touch-and-hold input. AssistiveTouch can also be found on this settings menu if you want alternative ways to control the screen, and the Accessibility ➝ Zoom menu includes an option to zoom using the touch display or Sidecar.


Whatever you think about touch on a Mac, one group with a genuine reason to leave it on is app developers. Xcode's iOS Simulator responds to direct touch, so you can test your app's taps, swipes, and pinches right on the screen instead of approximating them with a trackpad and keyboard modifiers.

title: Subscription scandal reveals the dark side of Apple’s pivot to services
content:
Macworld





Apple scandals usually revolve around a piece of hardware failing to do what it’s supposed to do: a phone, for instance, that loses connection, or bends in the pocket, or breaks when used normally. So the latest controversy is at least refreshingly different, in that hardware is barely involved at all.
For a couple of weeks now the consumer rights advocate Louis Rossman has been reporting on allegations of malpractice in Apple stores. (You can catch the gist in his latest video on the topic, while a fuller exploration is given in this earlier video.) It’s alleged, specifically, that multiple retail employees in multiple stores have signed up customers to auto-renewing subscription services without obtaining fully informed consent. And worse, that an employee performance metric put in place by Apple management incentivized them to do so.
Apple stores have a system called Connect and Personalize, under which purchasers of a new iPhone, iPad, or Mac scan a QR code to receive a tutorial from a retail employee. This process temporarily unlocks the customer’s account and payment information and shows the employee any free subscription trials for which the customer is eligible. Look, they will then say, you can get three months of Apple One (for example) for free; tap here to start your trial.
Like most services companies, Apple offers free trials not out of a sense of altruism but in the hopes that customers will carry on using the service after the trial ends. They are free to start with, then they auto-renew after a certain amount of time and the customer begins to pay. But whistleblowers claim the auto-renewal part of the deal was not always made clear to customers. Some employees implied that the trials were simply a gift with no strings; others, it is alleged, tapped Accept on their own device and didn’t get consent at all. Needless to say these are very serious allegations. We have contacted Apple for comment and will update this article to include the company’s response if we receive one.






While reports claim the practice is or has been relatively widespread (one tipster told Rossman that they had “confirmed with others that this happens at other stores” and that “many employees [have] admit[ted] to me that they do this”), one defense Apple could offer is that these were rogue employees taking matters into their own hands. That it wasn’t company policy to have employees behave in this way, and that company management is indeed aghast to hear about such goings-on.
But the issue with that defense is that the problem appears to be systemic. Not explicitly, and perhaps not intentionally, but indirectly as a result of employee incentives.
Apple, again like other companies, tracks the performance of its retail employees. Until recently, one metric by which performance was graded was called “services attach rate:” the percentage of device purchasers assisted by the employee who signed up for a subscription service. It’s been reported that employees in at least some stores were set a target of 40 percent. If you help 10 people buy iPads, you should make sure at least four of them sign up to something at the same time.
It isn’t clear what action was taken (or threatened) against employees who failed to meet this target, or whether there was a reward for those who did. But targets affect behavior even in the absence of explicit punishments and rewards. The mere existence of that 40 percent figure tells employees that the company values that specific form of success, and heavily implies that success or failure by this metric will be one of the factors used to determine promotions, redundancies, pay raises, and bonuses. It would be surreally naive to imagine that putting in place a target of this nature wouldn’t encourage employees to hard-sell signups and, in at least a few cases across an organization with more than 100,000 retail staff, bend the rules regarding informed consent.
Apple stopped tracking services attach rate shortly after Rossman’s reporting was published. This might be taken as a tacit acknowledgement that the metric was a bad idea with the potential to incentivise unethical behavior, but Apple claims it’s actually just a coincidence; the company told MacRumors the metric is simply “less relevant during the holiday season.” If that is truly the case, no doubt the metric will be reinstated in the new year.
The company has also reportedly sent internal memos to retail stores reminding employees to make sure they obtain informed consent before signing up customers to subscription trials, and to ensure it is customers, not the employees themselves, tapping the buttons. Again, this may or may not be a coincidence. Stores hire lots of new staff for the holiday season. Maybe it’s just a reminder for the newbies. But the timing is striking, to say the least.
Abuse the user: The dark side of services
Apple’s relentless march into services was one of the great successes of the Tim Cook era.
Overly dependent on the iPhone and trying to plan for the eventual decline of the smartphone market, the company pivoted: instead of just selling hardware, it would focus more and more on selling subscription services to people who own the hardware. This leads to steadier, more predictable recurring revenue and (assuming you own the services content, which Apple does wherever possible) effortless scalability. Building six million iPhone Duos is very difficult and expensive. Making one motor-racing movie is quite difficult and expensive, but distributing it to six million people barely increases your costs at all. At first glance it looks like a business model that’s all upside.
Services certainly have their advantages, and they’ve helped put Apple in a spectacularly strong financial position: this category brought in $30 billion of revenue in the last quarter alone. But selling subscriptions is a murkier business than selling one-off hardware purchases, because there’s more of a disconnect between the best outcomes for buyer and seller.
Selling hardware is essentially a collaborative effort, where both seller and buyer want the same thing: for the buyer to be pleased about the quality of the product and then buy the next model a year or two down the line. Sure, it’s a bit more complicated than that. We could talk about planned obsolescence, and unscrupulous retail employees encouraging people to buy a more powerful model than they need–although in both cases, short-term gain for the seller would come at the risk of long-term loss of user goodwill. In any case, because it’s a single purchase, the dynamic is relatively simple.
But when you switch to services, the best outcomes become radically decoupled. When it comes to streaming, for example, it’s clearly in the best interests of the customer to shop around, unsubscribe regularly, take a month of Netflix here and a month of Apple TV there. But it’s in the streamer’s interest for you to sign up and forget about it, like a gym owner who loses interest in your fitness journey the second you join. This is why whole seasons being dumped at once (which is good for the user) has largely been replaced by weekly drops, which is better for the streaming company.
If you pay for an iCloud+ subscription, similarly, your hope is that the storage allocation will prove adequate for your needs. Apple would much rather have your needs subtly increase, pushing you up to the next tier. If you pay for Apple Music, the company would ideally like for sharing to be a problem so you have to pay for the Family plan. Apple hasn’t yet put ads in these services, but (based on past behavior) it’s plausible that at some point it will follow the lead of Netflix and others and make the cheapest tier of TV+, Music, and Fitness+ ad-supported, thereby ensuring additional revenue while pushing customers to pay more for a higher tier.
Services, in short, reward companies which deliver a user-hostile experience.
An opportunity to be better
Apple has been making and selling tech hardware for 50 years; Apple Music didn’t open until 2015. So, when it comes to services, the company has had far less of a chance to forge an identity.
This, then, is an opportunity. Just as it did in desktops, laptops, music players and smartphones, Apple can establish itself as the services company that’s different. The one that begins with the idea of a great user experience and then extrapolates from that, rather than just doing whatever scrapes the most data or boosts engagement or increases short-term revenue.
Goodness knows there’s plenty of public discontent with the practices of streaming companies. There are swathes of streamers out there crying out for a provider which doesn’t constantly put up prices, deluge the user with unskippable adverts, remove content without warning, and cancel shows without giving them a chance. That could be Apple. It could also be the one company which doesn’t get flack for making it easy to sign up to a subscription and incredibly hard to end one.
Instead, many customers’ first experience with Apple as a services company is going into a store, paying a small fortune for a product, and then getting pushed into signing up to a subscription they don’t want or need. As first impressions go, it’s hard to think of a worse one. Be better, Apple.

title: Criminals are using government-grade spyware to infect iPhones
content:
Sophisticated iPhone spyware once reserved for government surveillance is now being used by cybercriminals against ordinary users, with a new security report finding that criminal attacks account for most of its detections.

iPhone 18
The findings come from mobile security firm iVerify's Advanced Mobile Threat Report 2026, published November 10. Researchers found 1.07 spyware infections per 1,000 consumer iOS scans, or roughly one in 900, while the rate dropped to 0.7 per 1,000 when enterprise devices were included.
The figures reflect iVerify's users, not the global iPhone population. Its consumer base has more than tripled since early 2025, although the report doesn't disclose total scans or infections.
The bigger shift is who's being targeted. Every enterprise infection linked to a criminal campaign involved a rank-and-file employee, not a high-profile executive.

title: OLED iPad Air Rumored to Launch in Two Sizes in Early 2027
content:
Apple is expected to replace the LCD screens in both sizes of the iPad Air with OLED displays in the first half of 2027, according to DigiTimes.


An ‌OLED‌ ‌iPad Air‌ has been rumored for over a year. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported in October 2025 that Apple was developing one and that it was unlikely to arrive before 2027. He narrowed that window to the first half of 2027 earlier this month. The latest report adds shipment estimates and details on how panel orders could be split.

seeking orders for one of the two sizes and still needs to qualify as a supplier. With orders for the ‌iPad Air‌ and iPad mini, Samsung could become Apple's largest supplier of ‌OLED‌ iPad panels overall, while LG Display is expected to retain the lead for the iPad Pro.

DigiTimes put 2027 shipments at 4 million to 5 million units each for the ‌iPad Air‌ and ‌iPad mini‌, and 3 million to 4 million for the ‌iPad Pro‌. The ‌iPad Air‌ and ‌iPad Pro‌ estimates each cover both screen sizes. The ‌iPad Pro‌ forecast is well below its reported pre-launch target of around 10 million units per year, with industry sources pointing to the price as a factor in weaker demand.

current M4 iPad Air use LCD screens. The move to ‌OLED‌ would make the ‌iPad Air‌ Apple's third ‌iPad‌ line to adopt the technology, following the ‌iPad Pro‌ in 2024 and the 8.5-inch iPad mini that went on sale November 6.

‌DigiTimes‌, the ‌iPad Air‌ is expected to use the same single-stack ‌OLED‌ design and low-temperature polycrystalline silicon (LTPS) backplane as the ‌iPad mini‌. ‌DigiTimes‌ previously reported that the ‌OLED‌ ‌iPad Air‌ would stick with 60Hz, leaving ProMotion exclusive to the ‌iPad Pro‌ in Apple's tablet lineup.

title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro guide: What to know before you buy
content:
Macworld





Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro is now on sale. Officially called MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the new lineup went on sale on November 6, 2026, with the first preorder deliveries arriving the same day.
The biggest changes include Dynamic Island, a smaller and lighter enclosure, and a new 16TB maximum SSD option on M5 Max configurations. The display adds Adobe RGB support and higher peak brightness while retaining a maximum 120Hz refresh rate. Other features include up to 128GB of RAM, Thunderbolt 5, Wi-Fi 7 and audio with a claimed 50% deeper bass.
The touchscreen models retain the same chip families, memory capacities and advertised battery endurance as their equivalent non-touch M5 models, making this primarily an upgrade to the display, design and how users interact with their Mac. U.S. starting prices carry a $400 premium over equivalent non-touch versions, with the 14-inch M5 Pro starting at $2,899 and the 16-inch M5 Max starting at $4,799.
What’s new compared with the non-touchscreen MacBook Pro?
The processor generation, maximum RAM, Thunderbolt generation, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth versions and Apple’s battery-life ratings haven’t changed, but there is a lot that is different.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro price
Apple has introduced a more expensive touchscreen range alongside the existing models. The new range carries a $400 starting-price premium over every equivalent non-touch M5 model. The premium does not buy a newer processor generation, more base memory or a larger entry SSD.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro design

				
					

				
			That’s a touchscreen Mac. Despite the wallpaper used for Apple’s image, the screen isn’t actually broken. 
Apple




The new MacBook Pro retains a conventional laptop layout, built-in keyboard and Force Touch trackpad. It comes in Space Black or Silver, with an enclosure made from 100% recycled aluminium. 
Compared to the existing models, the weight reduction is more substantial than the thickness reduction: the 14-inch models lose 220g, while the 16-inch models lose approximately 310–320g. Slimmer borders also allow the larger screen to grow slightly despite a reduced enclosure footprint.
Apple describes a revised hinge and cooling system. It claims greater hinge stability during touch input and says the cooling design directs warm air away from the display. In our initial testing, we found that ordinary taps caused slight but tolerable screen wobble. 
The illuminated Apple logo also returns on the PROLED XDR models. It lights up while the Mac is awake, adjusting to both the built-in display’s brightness and ambient lighting. There is no dedicated switch in System Settings, but Apple provides a Terminal command to disable it.

Touchscreen MacBook display

				
					

				
			The PROLED XDR Display isn’t just for touching.  

Stephan Wiesend




Both sizes offer M5 Pro and M5 Max configurations, and every PROLED XDR model includes touch. There is no base-M6 configuration in this touchscreen range.
OLED’s benefits concern image reproduction: individually lit pixels, deeper blacks and reduced blooming around bright objects. Touch adds a separate benefit – direct interaction with content. The maximum refresh rate remains 120Hz.
Apple indicates that pixel compensation mitigates ageing and burn-in, rather than establishing that OLED cannot deteriorate. It quotes 1% reflectance for standard glass; nano-texture scatters reflections further. 
In his review of the touchscreen MacBook Pro, Roman Loyola found the standard-glass display comfortable to use in direct sunlight. 
There is also an oleophobic coating to reduce fingerprints. For cleaning, Apple advises powering down and using a soft cloth appropriately dampened for standard screens; never spray liquid directly onto the display. For nano-texture, use the supplied polishing cloth and follow Apple’s specific care instructions.

Which MacBook models get a touchscreen?
Touch comes with the 14- and 16-inch PROLED XDR models using M5 Pro or M5 Max; the M6 MacBook Pro and Liquid Retina XDR models have no touchscreen.


						

							


How does touch work in macOS?

				
					

				
			Here’s what it’s like to use the touchscreen. 
Roman Loyola/Foundry




Apple confirms scrolling, pinch-to-zoom, drawing, dragging and dropping, double-tapping a window to fill the screen, and flicking windows into tiled positions. Touch works alongside keyboard and trackpad input.
Dynamic Island provides access to activities and controls. Spotlight’s relocation there requires Siri AI to be available and enabled. 
In everyday use, touch offers a direct way to move through documents, enlarge photographs or reposition content.
macOS translates taps into clicks for many existing apps; developers can use gesture APIs for more specialised controls. Apple has begun rolling out Creator Studio updates, which it says will illustrate how developers can use touch. Logic Pro 13 (updated November 5) gained onscreen instruments and drum pads, Final Cut Pro will support direct clip manipulation, and Pixelmator Pro will support drawing and selecting directly on the canvas. 
In his first look at the touchscreen MacBook Pro, Macworld’s Roman Loyola found touch responsive, with window controls enlarging and menus gaining extra spacing for fingers. Finder retains familiar Mac behavior: one tap selects an icon; two taps open it.
Some interactions need refinement. Roman found that double-tapping video files could trigger their icon previews instead of opening them. Fingerprints also accumulated despite the oleophobic coating, becoming most obvious when the display was dark. Read our touchscreen MacBook Pro first look for Roman’s hands-on impressions. 
In our full review of the touchscreen MacBook, touch worked across the apps Roman Loyola tried, but not in Resident Evil Village or Total War: Warhammer III, including the menus.
Apple indicated that there are forthcoming updates for Microsoft 365, Notion, Canva, Zoom, Lightroom, DaVinci Resolve, Blender, Cinema 4D, ZBrush, Shapr3D and djay Pro later this year. Creator Studio updates are confirmed to be coming in November.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro processor 
M5 Pro and M5 Max
As expected, the processors are carried-over M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. The new models feature the same CPU/GPU options, Neural Engine and memory bandwidth as the equivalent non-touch models.
Our testing found comparable processing performance to the equivalent non-touch M5 Max model.
All have a 16-core Neural Engine and GPU Neural Accelerators. The 18-core CPU comprises six “super cores” and 12 performance cores; the 15-core version has five and 10 respectively.
Apple introduced these chips earlier in 2026. They use third-generation 3nm manufacturing and Apple’s Fusion Architecture, joining two dies into one system-on-chip through advanced packaging. Those are characteristics of the existing M5 Pro/Max generation, not manufacturing upgrades introduced with touch. 
For an example of Apple’s older-generation comparisons, it claims 10.9× faster time to first token than M1 Pro for a 14-inch M5 Pro model. Apple’s test used an 18-core CPU/20-core GPU, 64GB RAM and 4TB SSD against an M1 Pro with 10-core CPU/16-core GPU, 32GB RAM and 8TB SSD. The workload was a quantised 14-billion-parameter model, an 8K-token prompt and LM Studio.
Apple made no indication that there was any CPU/GPU performance increase over an equivalent non-touch M5 configuration, or a quantified improvement in whole-system power efficiency. 
Separately, Apple has launched the 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook memory: How much RAM is included? 
There is no increase in base or maximum memory over the equivalent non-touch M5 models. The M5 Pro starts with 24GB, the 32-core GPU M5 Max has 36GB, and the 40-core version starts with 48GB.
Reaching 64GB with M5 Pro requires the 20-core GPU; reaching 128GB requires the 40-core M5 Max.
More memory can accommodate larger creative projects, more demanding multitasking and larger local AI models. 


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook storage: What is the highest capacity? 
Entry-level storage capacities are unchanged, but M5 Max buyers can now configure up to 16TB, up from 8TB, with either the 32-core or 40-core GPU.
The PROLED XDR models retain the SSD speed improvements introduced with the M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro earlier in 2026. Our review of the 16-inch M5 Max model with a 2TB SSD found noticeably faster read speeds than in our previous testing. Apple also claims storage is “up to twice as fast,” but that comparison is between a 16TB M5 Max system and an 8TB M4 Max system; it does not establish doubled performance over the non-touch M5 models.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook camera, microphones and speakers
The camera remains a 12MP Center Stage camera with Desk View and 1080p video recording. Advanced video stabilisation is new, however. 
Authentication remains Touch ID. Dynamic Island is an interface feature, not confirmation of Face ID or a TrueDepth camera.
Apple retains a six-speaker system, force-cancelling woofers, Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support. Apple claims 50% deeper bass and adds closed-lid audio tuning. 
The three-microphone array retains directional beamforming, Voice Isolation and Wide Spectrum modes. 


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook battery
Apple lists video-streaming ratings of 22/20 hours for the 14-inch Pro/Max and 24/22 hours for the 16-inch Pro/Max, the same as the non-touchscreen models. 
Our tested 16-inch M5 Max model, with a 40-core GPU and 128GB of memory, lasted approximately 24 hours looping a locally stored video at 150 nits. 


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro connectivity and ports 
Both sizes include:
One 3.5mm headphone jack with support for high-impedance headphones.
Three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C ports, supporting charging and DisplayPort.
One HDMI port.
One SDXC card slot.
MagSafe 3.
Apple quotes Thunderbolt/USB4 support up to 120Gb/s and DisplayPort 2.1. 
Apple’s N1 wireless chip, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread are included, but they are not touchscreen-model upgrades.
External display support
The M5 Pro chip supports three external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz. Alternatively, it can support one 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz display, plus a second at up to 5K/120Hz or 4K/200Hz.
The M5 Max chip supports four external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz, or two displays at up to 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz. 
Apple’s PROLED XDR specifications lists 165Hz for the multi-display 4K configurations, rather than the older 144Hz figure.

Should you buy the touchscreen MacBook Pro? 
Is touch worth the premium? Our full review found that the PROLED XDR display’s image quality is the strongest reason to pay extra. Touch is a useful addition, but the richer colors, deeper blacks and brighter OLED screen make this an appealing upgrade even if you prefer using the keyboard and trackpad. Whether those improvements and the lighter design justify the premium depends on how much you use the built-in display.
Which model? The 14-inch M5 Pro is the most accessible and portable option. Choose the 16-inch M5 Pro for a larger workspace and Apple’s longest battery rating. M5 Max makes sense when GPU performance, memory bandwidth, more than 64GB RAM or storage above 4TB serves a demonstrated workload; it is unnecessary simply to obtain touch.
Should existing owners upgrade? For owners of an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro, this is principally a screen and portability decision. M4 owners should similarly assess the display benefits against the cost. Older Apple-silicon and Intel owners may gain more broadly, but performance improvements vary by application.
This or an iPad Pro? Choose the MacBook Pro when desktop Mac applications, its keyboard, ports and professional workflows are essential. Choose an iPad Pro when a handheld tablet and supported Apple Pencil workflow are central. The touchscreen MacBook Pro supports finger input but does not support Apple Pencil or third-party styli. It retains a conventional laptop design.

title: The Original iPod Went on Sale 25 Years Ago Today
content:
Apple's original iPod went on sale 25 years ago today, on November 10, 2001. The $399 music player initially worked only with a Mac, but it went on to become one of Apple's most significant products and helped the company expand beyond the computer business.


Steve Jobs had unveiled the first iPod just over two weeks earlier, on October 23, at a small press event in the Town Hall auditorium at Apple's Infinite Loop headquarters. Advertised as offering "1,000 songs in your pocket," the device combined a 5GB hard drive with a monochrome LCD display, a mechanical scroll wheel, and up to 10 hours of battery life.

The original model required iTunes. Its FireWire connection transferred music and charged the battery, while automatic synchronization copied songs and playlists from the user's iTunes library. Apple said that an entire CD could be transferred in under 10 seconds and a collection of 1,000 songs in less than 10 minutes. The hard drive could also store documents and other files.

MacRumors rumor roundup published two days before the event included the name "iPod."




original coverage is still available, along with reader comments questioning the device's price, Mac-only compatibility, and significance. One reader described it as "far from revolutionary," while another wrote, "all this hype for something so ridiculous!" Early forum discussions also covered fingerprints on the polished rear enclosure, heat while charging, and the sound quality of the included earbuds.

Hardware revisions followed in quick succession. The second-generation iPod adopted a touch-sensitive scroll wheel, while the third-generation model introduced the 30-pin Dock Connector in 2003. The full-size iPod gained a color display in 2004 and video playback in 2005.

The iPod mini was announced in January 2004, representing the first extension of the product line. It featured a smaller anodized aluminum enclosure in silver, gold, pink, blue, or green, and introduced the Click Wheel, which integrated playback buttons into the touch-sensitive scrolling surface. Apple adopted the same control for the fourth-generation full-size iPod later that year.



In 2005, Apple introduced both the iPod shuffle and iPod nano. The shuffle omitted a display and offered a smaller, simpler music player, while the nano replaced the mini with a thin design based on flash storage. Later iPod nano models added video playback, a video camera, and a touchscreen. The square sixth-generation model, introduced in 2010, could be worn on the wrist using third-party watch straps.

sold 100 million iPods, less than six years after the first model reached customers. By October 2011, sales had exceeded 304 million units.

iPod touch arrived in September 2007, several months after the first iPhone went on sale. It featured a 3.5-inch Multi-Touch display, Wi-Fi, and Safari, without requiring a cellular plan.



iPod classic in September 2014, five years after its final hardware revision. The iPod nano and iPod shuffle followed in July 2017, leaving the iPod touch as the sole model.

announced its discontinuation and said it would be available while supplies lasted.

announcement, Apple attributed the end of the lineup to the integration of music playback across its other products. Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing, said that "the spirit of iPod lives on" through devices including the iPhone, Apple Watch, HomePod mini, Mac, iPad, and Apple TV.

title: Apple TV 4K needs a downgrade
content:
Macworld





After two years, Apple will finally start shipping its new generation of Apple TV 4K this week, and while it comes with some nice improvements — like a faster chip — there’s something else that made headlines. The new model is much more expensive than the previous model, now starting at $299. Yes, there’s a lot to like about the new Apple TV. But while Apple has made its streaming box better, I’m not convinced the product is heading in the right direction.
Don’t get me wrong. I’ve always liked Apple’s set-top box. In fact, I think tvOS has one of the best interfaces of any streaming platform. But instead of making the Apple TV more accessible to more people, Apple keeps adding more powerful hardware and charging more for it. The problem is, most people don’t really need that power, and Apple itself doesn’t even take full advantage of it.
Does Apple TV really need all that power?
The main upgrade in the new Apple TV 4K is the A19 chip — the same one found in the iPhone 17. Benchmarks show a 50 percent gain in CPU speed and double the graphics performance between the new chip and the A15 from the previous Apple TV. That’s an impressive leap, but the thing is, do you really need all that power just to watch TV?
Most people who own an Apple TV don’t use it for much more than watching movies and TV shows. Apps like Netflix, YouTube, or even Apple TV don’t need that much power. Even if you occasionally use AirPlay or play a light game from Apple Arcade, you probably won’t have any performance issues with older Apple TV models. Sure, the A19 brings some meaningful improvements, including more efficient video decoding, but I find it hard to believe that most people will notice this upgrade on an Apple TV.
Even Apple is having a hard time justifying the upgrade. In the press release announcing the new Apple TV 4K, it says that the A19 chip enables “greater responsiveness, faster navigation, and smoother animations.” That doesn’t sound convincing enough to me to buy a new Apple TV. I’m all for making a product faster, but there’s a point where adding more power stops making a meaningful difference to the experience.

				
					

				
			
An older Apple TV 4K is plenty powerful for streaming.

Foundry




Nothing new
The biggest problem with Apple TV isn’t having powerful hardware, but the cost that comes with it. Previous Apple TV models were already powerful enough for a streaming box, but they were somewhat cheap. When it was $129, it was easy to justify buying one. But at $299, Apple TV is getting dangerously close to the price of a whole television. For about the same price, you can buy something that comes with a large screen, built-in speakers, and access to streaming apps.
Of course, I know the experience isn’t the same. Cheap smart TVs often have terrible software and annoying advertisements. Some manufacturers also have a bad reputation when it comes to software updates. That’s why I and so many others swear by Apple TV and tvOS in the first place. It makes using a television much more enjoyable. But is that experience really worth $300? Just a few months ago, you could buy an Apple TV and a pair of HomePod minis to use as speakers for $327. Now that same amount of money will only get you the streaming box.
Of course, for those immersed in the Apple ecosystem, Apple TV still makes sense. You can use it with your HomePods and as a hub for HomeKit accessories. It becomes more than just a streaming device. The new Apple TV, for example, lets you set up a surround sound system with four HomePods. These are all welcome additions, sure, but they also make Apple TV even more of a niche product.
Meanwhile, Amazon, Roku, and other competitors offer streaming devices that are a lot cheaper. Their software certainly isn’t as good as tvOS, but they get the job done for many people.

				
					

				
			
An underpowered streaming device like the Fire TV Stick is just what Apple needs.

Jared Newman / Foundry




What we really need is an Apple TV stick




A faster Apple TV doesn’t really offer any benefits to most users. The truth is, it’s getting harder and harder to justify buying an Apple TV when smart TVs get better every year. 
At the same time, I don’t think Apple should completely ditch the premium Apple TV. There’s clearly a market for it. However, as memory and storage prices continue to increase, Apple should also offer a cheaper model for those who just want a nice way to use their favorite streaming apps.
I’d love to see an Apple TV Stick. Something like a smaller device that runs tvOS and costs half as much as the current generation. It just needs to run tvOS and stream 4K smoothly, without the latest chip or built-in microphones. Apple TV is great, but it doesn’t need to become more powerful. It needs to become more affordable.

title: How Steve Jobs saved Apple with the online Apple Store
content:
Alongside the return of Steve Jobs, Apple's first online store played a crucial role in the company's survival and resurgence. It officially opened for business on November 10, 1997 and has been online ever since — except when Apple takes it offline to promote the launch of new products.


Detail from an early appearance of the Apple Store online
It wasn't enough that Steve Jobs came back to Apple and stripped its messy range down to a few core products. The iMac wasn't enough to turn the company around either — not by itself. While it may not have seemed it at the time, the launch of the online Apple Store on November 10, 1997 turned out to be crucial component of the company's survival.
There's an argument that it was born of irritation rather than anyone seeing how useful it would be. But while there is truth in that, the full story is that Apple badly needed its own online store.

title: Waze Now Alerts Drivers to Nearby Cyclists Using Garmin LiveTrack
content:
Waze and Garmin have announced the launch of real-time cycling alerts for drivers to help create a safer environment on the road.


Going forward, when cyclists turn on Garmin LiveTrack on their Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch, they can choose to show up in Waze as a real-time moving icon. 

Drivers will also see a notification when a cyclist is nearby, so they can slow down, stay aware, and share the road.

The feature is completely opt-in, and Waze and Garmin say it is designed with privacy in mind. Drivers only see a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby, and a cyclist's name, identity, or exact route is never shared in the app. Alerts also automatically turn off the moment a cyclist ends their ride on the Garmin device.
