The MacBook Air (M5) is the best MacBook for most buyers because it offers the strongest balance of price, portability, battery life, and performance.
The 13-inch MacBook Air is light, quiet, fast enough for everyday work, and easier to recommend than any other Mac laptop. The latest version, updated in March 2026, keeps the same winning formula while improving storage and connectivity. There is also a 15-inch version for anyone who wants a larger screen. 
What’s new
The latest MacBook Air features the M5 chip, base storage is 512GB, and it supports newer wireless standards including Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
Why we recommend the MacBook Air
Excellent balance of performance and portability
Silent fanless design
Long battery life
Strong everyday performance for work, school, and travel
Now ships with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage as standard
Sizes
The MacBook Air comes in two sizes:
13-inch MacBook Air, 13.6-inch screen: Best for portability
15-inch MacBook Air, 15.3-inch screen: Better for multitasking and split-screen work
Display
As you can see from the above measurements, the display, when measured diagonally is a little larger than the standard naming would suggest. As a result the 13-inch MacBook Air display is actually larger than that on the 13-inch MacBook Neo, discussed below. The MacBook Air uses a bright Liquid Retina display, but it still lacks the 120Hz ProMotion refresh rate and HDR capabilities found on MacBook Pro models.
Performance
The M5 chip in the MacBook Air is fast enough for office work, school tasks, web apps, multitasking, and light creative work. Because the Air has no fan, though, performance can dip during long video exports or other sustained heavy workloads so that the temperature remains optimal.
Battery life
Battery life is excellent, making the Air a great choice for anyone who works away from a desk. It offers more battery life than the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, but falls short of the 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
Other specs
You get MagSafe 3 for charging and two Thunderbolt 4 ports. The MacBook Air also supports up to two external displays. (Older M1 and M2 models were limited to one external monitor). 
16GB RAM to 32GB RAM
From 512GB to 4TB SSD
Price
Apple put MacBook Air prices up by $200 in June 2026. 
13-inch MacBook Air: Now starts at $1,299/£1,299
15-inch MacBook Air: Now starts at $1,499/£1,499
What to know before buying
The Air’s biggest limitation is sustained performance. It is quick for most tasks, but it is not the right machine for users who regularly push their system for long periods. The MacBook Air is likely to soon adopt the M6 chip as used in the entry-level MacBook Pro, Mac mini and iMac.

The MacBook Neo is the cheapest way to buy a Mac laptop in 2026. Now starting at $699 (which is unfortunately $100 more than it was when Apple launched it in March), it is aimed at students, first-time Mac buyers, and casual users who mainly browse the web, stream video, join video calls, and work in basic apps.
Despite its lower price, it still looks and feels like a MacBook, with an all-aluminum design and a lightweight chassis.
Who is MacBook Neo for?
The MacBook Neo is best for people whose computing needs are simple: web browsing, email, documents, streaming, and schoolwork.
Why we recommend MacBook Neo
Lowest price in the lineup

Sizes

13-inch MacBook Neo, 13-inch screen
Display 
Like the MacBook Air the MacBook Neo offers a Liquid Retina display with max 500 nits brightness, but that’s where the similarities end. The display is slightly smaller than the display on the 13-inch MacBook Air, offering 2,408 by 1,506 pixels compared to 2,560 by 1,664 pixels. It also lacks the wide color P3 and True Tone technology of the other MacBooks, offering only sRGB color. 
Performance 
The MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip – the same processor first introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro. While it is a mobile-class chip, its performance is optimized for a laptop environment, offering a highly responsive experience for everyday productivity. In our tests it proved faster than the M3 in single-core, while equal to the M1 when it came to multi-core performance and graphics. 
Battery life 
The MacBook Neo should comfortably last a working day of general productivity. In our video-loop battery test, with screen brightness set to 150 nits, it lasted 13 hours and 15 minutes. Apple advertises up to 16 hours of video streaming or 11 hours of wireless web browsing. More demanding tasks will drain the battery faster.
Other specs
You get two USB-C ports, but these are not identical in capability, one being USB 3 and the other USB 2. See MacBook Neo ports explained. The MacBook Neo only supports one external display with a resolution of up to 4K at 60Hz.

What to know before buying
The Neo makes several trade-offs to achieve its low price, including the absence of a backlit keyboard, a limited selection of ports, and no Touch ID on the base model. It also features a lower-quality display compared to the Air and Pro, offers less memory with a maximum of 8GB RAM, and delivers lower sustained performance than M-series MacBooks. For many buyers, the 512GB, $799 model represents better value, as it includes Touch ID and additional storage.
Alternatives
The MacBook Neo is the best budget MacBook, but it is best suited to light workloads. If you can spend more, the MacBook Air remains the better long-term buy for most people.
Another option, if a low price is your top priority, is a refurbished MacBook. Look out for clearance deals on older Apple silicon MacBooks, but avoid the older Intel-based models. See: MacBook Pro deals and MacBook Air deals.

Up to 16TB of storage with M5 Max
Sizes
There are two sizes to choose from:
14-inch MacBook Pro, 14.2-inch screen: The more portable option, starting at 1.38kg.
16-inch MacBook Pro, 16.3-inch screen: More workspace for creative apps, starting at 1.82kg.
Display
Both sizes feature a tandem OLED PROLED XDR touchscreen. Apple specifies up to 1,000 nits sustained full-screen brightness and 2,000 nits peak brightness for HDR content and outdoor SDR use.
The display supports P3 and Adobe RGB color, True Tone and ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. Dynamic Island replaces the notch.
In our review of the 16-inch model, the screen’s richer colors, deeper blacks and brightness stood out as the strongest reasons to upgrade—even if you prefer using the keyboard and trackpad.
Touch provides another way to scroll, zoom and interact with content. It worked in the Apple and third-party apps Roman tested, although Resident Evil Village and Total War: Warhammer III did not support it, including in their menus and setup screens.
Performance
Choose between the same chip families offered in the non-touchscreen professional models:
M5 Pro: Suitable for demanding photo editing, software development, video editing and heavier multitasking.
M5 Max: For more intensive graphics, high-end video production, 3D work and workloads requiring larger memory configurations.
Choose the chip around your workload, then decide whether the display and lighter design justify the extra cost.
Battery life
Apple advertises the same video-streaming endurance as equivalent non-touchscreen models:
14-inch M5 Pro: Up to 22 hours.
14-inch M5 Max: Up to 20 hours.
16-inch M5 Pro: Up to 24 hours.
16-inch M5 Max: Up to 22 hours.
These figures are Apple’s ratings, rather than our independent test results. In our testing, the 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, an M5 Max chip, 40-core GPU and 128GB of memory lasted approximately 24 hours looping a locally stored video with screen brightness set to 150 nits. 
Other specs
M5 Pro: From 24GB to 64GB unified memory, depending on configuration; 1TB to 4TB SSD.
M5 Max: From 36GB to 128GB unified memory, depending on configuration; 2TB to 16TB SSD.
Three Thunderbolt 5 ports, HDMI, SDXC, MagSafe and a headphone jack.
Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
Price
Starting prices are:
14-inch M5 Pro: $2,899/£2,899.
16-inch M5 Pro: $3,399/£3,399.
14-inch M5 Max: $4,499/£4,499.
16-inch M5 Max: $4,799/£4,799.
Each starts at $400/£400 more than its equivalent non-touchscreen model.
What to know before buying
The combination of OLED, touch and reduced weight may justify the premium if you regularly work on the built-in screen. If you mainly use an external monitor, a non-touchscreen model could offer better value.
Our full review found that screen quality is the strongest reason to choose the PROLED XDR model. Our reviewer Roman Loyola praised its brightness, richer colors and deeper blacks, making it an appealing upgrade even if you prefer using the keyboard and trackpad. Touch is a useful addition, but you don’t need to use it to appreciate the better display.


MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro: Which should you buy?

				
					

				
			
The M5 MacBook Air and M6 MacBook Pro are different in some significant ways.

Foundry




The MacBook Air is our recommendation for most people, offering enough performance for everyday work and light creative projects in a thin, light, silent design. Choose the MacBook Pro if you regularly run demanding workloads or will benefit from its better display and additional ports.
The closest comparison is between the M5 MacBook Air and 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. For more demanding professional work, the MacBook Pro also offers M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, with a choice of non-touchscreen or PROLED XDR touchscreen displays.
Performance: Do you need a MacBook Pro?
The M5 MacBook Air is well suited to web browsing, office apps, studying, photo editing, and occasional video projects. Using creative software doesn’t automatically mean you need a Pro: the size of your projects and how frequently you run demanding tasks matter more.
The M6 MacBook Pro combines a newer chip generation with active cooling. Its fans help it sustain performance during lengthy video exports, code compilation, and other intensive tasks. The Air’s fanless design keeps it completely silent, but performance can fall during prolonged heavy workloads.
If these demanding tasks make up much of your working day, consider an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro. These offer greater processing, graphics, and memory capacity than the standard M6 model. A newer chip generation doesn’t automatically make the M6 the more powerful choice.
Display and ports: What does the Pro add?
The MacBook Air’s Liquid Retina display is suitable for everyday work, with 500 nits brightness and a 60Hz refresh rate. You can choose a 13-inch model for portability or a 15-inch model for more workspace.
The M6 MacBook Pro’s 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display adds mini-LED technology, deeper contrast, brighter HDR highlights, and ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. These features are particularly useful for viewing and editing HDR content, although you don’t need to be a creative professional to appreciate the screen.
The M6 Pro also provides three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot. The Air has two Thunderbolt 4 ports, so connecting memory cards, HDMI displays, or several accessories may require adapters or a dock.
For an OLED touchscreen, choose a PROLED XDR MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. Touchscreen availability is a separate consideration from how much processing power you need.
Portability, battery life, and price
The Air is thinner and lighter, making it the stronger choice if you carry your laptop regularly. The 15-inch Air is also worth considering if you want a larger screen without the weight and expense of a 16-inch Pro.
The M6 MacBook Pro has a higher advertised battery-life rating, although actual endurance depends on your workload. Both models are suitable for working away from a power socket.
The Air costs less, but compare configurations with matching memory and storage before deciding. The M6 Pro starts with more storage, which narrows the price difference if you would otherwise upgrade the Air.
Our buying advice: Air or Pro?
Buy the MacBook Air for everyday work, studying, travel, and light creative projects. It offers the best balance of performance, portability, and price for most buyers.
Buy the M6 MacBook Pro if you want its HDR display, additional ports, longer advertised battery life, or better sustained performance.
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro for demanding professional workloads that justify more processing power, graphics performance, or memory. Consider the PROLED XDR version if you also want OLED and touch.

While Windows PCs still hold a performance lead in raw frames per second, Apple Silicon has made high-end gaming a viable reality on macOS, particularly with the latest Pro and Max models. 
The M5 Pro MacBook Pro, updated in March 2026, strikes a balance for those who need “oomph” for gaming without the extreme price tag of the M5 Max version of the MacBook Pro. 
It includes Thunderbolt 5 ports for high-speed data transfer and supports more unified memory than the base M5. It is specifically recommended for “serious gaming” and moderate media production.
The M5 Pro model lacks the massive GPU core count of the Max chip, meaning it may struggle with the highest settings on the most demanding AAA titles like Cyberpunk 2077.
In our real-world gaming benchmarks, it provides “good results” for Mac users, even if it still faces a gap compared to dedicated PC gaming rigs.

Is MacBook Air good enough?

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




The MacBook Air may suffice in some cases: 
Creatives: The Air works well for light creative work, especially photo editing, design, and shorter video projects. It is not as strong in sustained workloads, but it is much easier to carry and costs less.
Development: The MacBook Air is still a good choice for lighter software development, especially for web development, scripting, and general programming. It is best for developers who prioritize portability over maximum sustained speed.
Gaming: The M5 MacBook Air features a third-generation ray-tracing engine and enhanced shader cores, which Apple says improves 3D rendering and gaming tasks. However, in our tests the lack of active cooling caused performance to dip after playing for 10 minutes or so. You can play casual games just fine, but for a variety of reasons, if you’re into AAA gaming, the Air isn’t the best choice.
What about MacBook Neo?
If your budget is much tighter and your needs are basic, the MacBook Neo is the entry point. It gives you macOS at a much lower price, but with more compromises than the Air. If you choose the Neo we recommend the 512GB version.

Other MacBook buying decisions to consider
When buying a MacBook, it’s important to consider how you will use it, as this will determine the right balance of performance, portability, and price. 
Key factors to consider include which chip you require, how much RAM you will need for multitasking, and the size of the SSD required for storage, all of which cannot be upgraded later. 
Screen size affects portability and productivity, screen quality is key for creative work, while battery life matters if you work on the go. You should also think about weight, port selection, and long-term value to ensure the device meets your needs both now and in the future.
In the next section we’ll examine these elements of the buying decision. 






Best MacBook display and screen size

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The best MacBook screen size depends on how much portability, screen space, and display quality you need.
Best MacBook screen sizes

Best size for portability: 13-inch MacBook Air or MacBook Neo 
Best all-around Pro size: 14-inch MacBook Pro 
Best large-screen option without Pro pricing: 15-inch MacBook Air 
Best for maximum workspace: 16-inch MacBook Pro 
How many screens are supported 
The 13-inch and 14-inch MacBooks offer the best balance of portability and usability. The larger 15-inch and 16-inch options are ideal if you want more room for spreadsheets, side-by-side apps, or general multitasking. These displays can run alongside the built-in screen. The M5 Pro and M5 Max limits apply to both touchscreen and non-touchscreen models.

MacBook Pro (M5 Max): Supports up to four external displays, each at 6K/60Hz.
For more advice read: How to use two or more monitors to a Mac.
MacBook displays: Liquid Retina, Liquid Retina XDR and PROLED XDR
Apple’s MacBooks offer three main display types. The most useful differences are brightness, contrast, refresh rate and touchscreen support.
Liquid Retina: MacBook Neo and MacBook Air
These displays suit everyday work, web browsing and watching videos. They have a fixed 60Hz refresh rate and don’t support touch. The Air’s display also supports the wider P3 color gamut, making it a better choice than the Neo for color-sensitive work.
Liquid Retina XDR: Non-touchscreen MacBook Pro
The M6 MacBook Pro and non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models use mini-LED displays. These offer higher contrast and brighter HDR highlights than the Air, plus ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother scrolling and motion.
PROLED XDR: Touchscreen MacBook Pro
The touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models use OLED displays. OLED controls light at the individual pixel level, producing deep blacks without the backlight blooming that can occur with mini-LED. These models also support direct touchscreen input.

Is the touchscreen MacBook Pro worth paying extra for?
The touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $400/£400 more than an equivalent non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max model. That premium buys display and design improvements, with the same processor options.
What the premium gets you
A tandem OLED display: The PROLED XDR screen offers higher contrast and adds Adobe RGB alongside P3 color support. This may be particularly valuable for photographers, video editors and designers who regularly use the built-in display.
Touchscreen input: Scroll, pinch to zoom and interact directly with content onscreen, alongside the keyboard and trackpad. Its usefulness will depend on your apps and how you prefer to work.
A thinner, lighter design: The 14-inch model weighs approximately half a pound less than its non-touch equivalent. Both sizes also replace the notch with Dynamic Island.
When it’s worth the extra money
The premium is easiest to justify if you spend much of your working day using the laptop’s own screen. The combination of OLED, wider color support and touch could make it a more useful workspace, while the reduced weight benefits anyone who frequently carries their MacBook.
You don’t have to want touch to appreciate the other improvements. As Macworld’s Roman Loyola argues, the display may be the more compelling upgrade.
When to choose a non-touch model
If you mainly work with an external monitor, the upgraded built-in display offers less benefit. A non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max can provide the processing power and memory you need at a lower price.
Touch also won’t suit every workflow. Reaching across the keyboard may be less comfortable than using the trackpad for extended periods, so consider how often you would actually use it.
Compare matching chip, memory and storage configurations before deciding: retailer discounts could make the price difference larger than $400/£400.






Which is the best MacBook for battery life?
The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro and 16-inch M5 Pro MacBook Pro share Apple’s highest advertised video-streaming rating, at up to 24 hours. For wireless web browsing, the 16-inch M5 Pro leads at up to 17 hours.
The MacBook Air offers a lighter, less expensive option, with both sizes rated for up to 18 hours of video streaming or 15 hours of web browsing. The budget-friendly MacBook Neo has lower advertised endurance, at 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively.

How much RAM do you need?
For most buyers in 2026, 16GB of RAM should be the minimum. That is the sweet spot for a MacBook you plan to keep for several years. 
However, the MacBook Neo ships with only 8GB RAM, and there are no options to upgrade this capacity at the time of purchase or later. Whether this is enough RAM depends entirely on your specific use case, as the device is positioned as a budget-friendly entry point into the Mac ecosystem. For the target audience – students, teachers, and casual users – 8GB of RAM should be sufficient for general productivity. A significant concern regarding the 8GB capacity is its long-term viability. 
MacBook memory is not upgradeable after purchase. If you expect to keep your laptop for a long time, it is worth buying more RAM upfront if your budget allows.
RAM recommendations by user type
Casual users and students: 16GB recommended. 8GB is workable for very light use, but not ideal for longevity.
Creative work and gaming: 24GB to 32GB is the safer target.

How much storage do you need for a MacBook?
256GB: Fine for cloud-first users with light local storage needs, but it can fill up quickly.
512GB: The better starting point for most people. It gives you more breathing room for apps, files, photos, and offline media.
1TB or more: Best for media professionals, developers with larger local workloads, or anyone who works with large files regularly.
Determining the best storage capacity for a MacBook depends heavily on your specific workflow, as internal storage cannot be upgraded after purchase. 
While Apple previously offered 256GB as a baseline, most current models now start at 512GB or 1TB to accommodate the increasing space requirements of modern operating systems and applications. For most buyers, 512GB is the practical minimum if the budget allows.
Experts now generally advise against 256GB drives for primary machines. Furthermore, SSDs can slow down significantly as they fill up. A common rule of thumb is to buy at least twice the capacity of what you need to store to maintain performance.
Storage (SSD) recommendations by user type
Casual users and students: 512GB recommended. Sufficient for documents, web browsing, and light media use.
General Productivity: 512GB to 1TB recommended. For users with moderate photo libraries and some video projects.
Creative Professionals: 1TB to 2TB+ recommended. Necessary for 4K video editing, large high-resolution photo libraries, and professional audio suites.
High-End Workflows: 4TB to 8TB recommended. For 3D animation, AI development, and massive video production projects.
Is there a difference between SSDs in Apple’s MacBooks
There are significant differences in SSD performance, capacity, and technology across the current MacBook lineup. In March 2026, Apple introduced faster storage technologies for the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models. 
The most notable differences lie in the read/write speeds, which vary based on the model’s processor and the physical capacity of the drive:
MacBook Pro (M5 Pro/Max): The M5 Pro and Max models, released in March 2026, feature the fastest internal storage in the lineup. Apple claims these SSDs are up to twice as fast as the previous generation. 
MacBook Pro (M6): Apple describes the SSD in the M6 model as “Superfast”. With the arrival of the M5 in 2025 Apple claimed it delivered up to 2x faster read/write performance than its predecessors.
MacBook Air (M5): The M5 MacBook Air also received a similar storage speed boost with the March 2026 update. 
MacBook Neo: The MacBook Neo uses a slower SSD to maintain its lower price point.

 FAQ 


1.
Which MacBook lasts the longest?
For battery life, the MacBook Pro models lead the lineup, with 24 hours of playback.





2.
Should I buy a refurbished MacBook?
A refurbished MacBook can be a good value, especially if you buy Apple silicon rather than Intel. Just make sure the price gap is meaningful and the machine still has enough life left to justify the purchase.
Since Apple put up prices across the range buying in the Refurbished Store is even more attractive. The MacBook Air, MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro were all available at the original price shortly after Apple raised prices. 
For example, the MacBook Neo is $599, you can get a 13-inch, M5 MacBook Air for $1,099 and a 14-inch MacBook Pro, M5 Pro for $2,119.





3.
Is a MacBook Air powerful enough?
Yes. For most people, the MacBook Air is more than powerful enough for everyday work, school, multitasking, web use, and light creative tasks.





4.
Is a MacBook worth it compared to a Windows laptop?
That depends on your priorities, but MacBooks are often worth the extra cost if you value exceptional battery life, premium build quality, class-leading trackpads, and seamless integration with the Apple ecosystem.
Apple’s recent price increases have made Macs more expensive, but the company isn’t alone in raising prices. Lenovo also announced price rises in June 2026, while other PC manufacturers have warned that soaring memory and storage costs are putting pressure on margins, making higher prices increasingly likely across the industry. As a result, the price gap between Macs and comparable Windows laptops may not be as large as it first appears.





5.
How long will a MacBook last?
The typical lifespan of a MacBook is generally between five and eight years, though this depends heavily on a combination of hardware durability and ongoing software support . While the physical components are built to last, Apple eventually classifies older models as “vintage” or “obsolete,” which limits your ability to get official repairs and parts. Find out more here: How long do MacBooks last: Lifespan, support and when to upgrade.





Why you can trust Macworld

Nobody knows Apple better, except probably Apple, but the difference is that we are completely impartial. title: Singapore Saved Apple $2.7 Billion in Taxes This Year
content:
Apple paid more income tax in Ireland than in Singapore in fiscal 2026, but it saved more in Singapore.



annual report shows that the company paid $4.96 billion in cash income taxes in Ireland and $3.25 billion in Singapore. Against the 21% U.S. federal corporate tax rate, Singapore lowered Apple's tax expense by $2.67 billion, about $100 million more than Ireland did.

top-up tax erased nearly half of that initial saving. Singapore introduced the tax to bring the effective tax rate for qualifying large multinationals up to 15%.

new U.S. accounting rules. Apple reported a combined figure for its foreign subsidiaries in fiscal 2025 and 2024, so those years offer no direct comparison between Singapore and Ireland.

Financial Times estimated that Apple booked up to $50 billion in pretax profit in Singapore in 2026. Apple's Singapore subsidiaries reported nearly $40 billion a year earlier.

title: MacBook Pro With PROLED XDR Display: Details You Might Have Missed
content:
The new MacBook Pro models with PROLED XDR displays began arriving to customers on Friday, and various details about the laptops continue to surface.


Given these models are available with the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that power the models with mini-LED displays, performance was expected to be virtually identical across the board, and benchmark results confirm that is the case.

Geekbench 7 database:
16-inch MacBook Pro (Mini-LED, M5 Max): 34,988

16-inch MacBook Pro (PROLED XDR, M5 Max): 34,904
The chip has an 18-core CPU in both models.

YouTube channel Max Tech noted that the bottom cover on the new MacBook Pro models has slightly recessed feet, and there are now only four pentalobe screws holding it in place, compared to eight on previous models.

Under the bottom cover sit larger speakers, which provide 50% deeper bass according to Apple.

16-inch/Mini-LED on left, 16-inch/PROLED on right

While the MacBook Neo's keyboard can be replaced individually, this is not the case for the new MacBook Pro models, as Apple's repair manuals show the laptops continue to have an all-in-one "Top Case with Battery and Keyboard" part.

In case you missed it, the bottom corners of the display are now rounded on the new models, whereas only the top corners are rounded on the mini-LED displays. This small change results in a much more uniform design.


As we noted over the weekend, Daring Fireball's John Gruber confirmed that the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro lids uses a custom light source — seemingly a white LED. On older MacBooks released in 2015 and earlier, the Apple logo was illuminated by the LCD's backlight, but OLED displays do not have a backlight.

title: Apple’s new glowing logo on the MacBook Pro has a hidden on-off switch
content:
Macworld





With the MacBook Pro with PROLED Display, Apple returned the Apple logo to its former glory, switching from shiny aluminum to one that lights up and glows again. And it’s got a new trick: Turn up the display brightness, and the logo gets brighter, too. Turn down the display brightness, and the logo dims.
However, since the brightness controls on the display and logo are linked, the only way to turn the brightness on the logo all the way down is to also turn off the display. And sadly, Apple did not include a system setting control for the logo, so you can’t turn it off by simply flicking a switch.
But you can turn it off through Terminal, Apple’s command line interface for the Mac. In fact, Apple has a support document with the details.
Turn off the glowing Apple logo
You must be logged into the Mac with an account that has Administrator rights.
Launch Terminal. It is in Applications>Utilities. You can also press Command + Space to bring up Spotlight Search, type “Terminal,” and press Return after “Terminal — Open” appears in the search box.
Copy the following and paste it into Terminal sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0  then press Return
Terminal will ask for your password, which must be a user with Administrator rights. (When typing the password, Terminal will not show the characters.) Press Return and the logo should turn off.
Quit Terminal.
Turn on the glowing Apple logo
Follow the same steps as above, but enter this Terminal command: sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode 
The glowing Apple logo is on by default, so if you reinstall macOS after turning it off, it will turn back on.
Or use a new app
Fortunately, now, there’s an app for that. Juan Buis created Backglow, a utility that can be used to customize the glowing Apple logo. In addition to turning it off and on, the free version of Backglow provides settings for two different pulse modes and it can remove the brightness limit. If you pay $9 for Backglow Pro, it activates the ability to set the glow pulse to music, and use Claude Code for your own personal pulse modes.

				
					

				
			Backglow can reside in the menu bar for quick access.

title: Some HomePod Mini 2 Buyers Returning Units Over Mac Speaker Issues
content:
One of the features of Apple's new HomePod mini 2 speakers is being able to use them as your Mac's default speakers, but it seems to be failing to work as advertised for a number of users, with some owners already returning them, based on the latest MacRumors forum reports.

OG HomePod minis in a stereo pair on a Mac (don't try this at home)

The new HomePod mini 2 can be used as a default speaker on all Mac models with Wi-Fi 6E or later, according to Apple. A single HomePod can be used alone, or a pair can be twinned for stereo sound. The same setup never reliably worked with the first-generation HomePod mini, with latency and dropout issues common.

HomePod‌ Software 27.2, and it's meant to work over "a responsive and persistent AirPlay connection," or a wireless point-to-point link that's designed to survive restarts and sleep. (That's different to ordinary AirPlay, which the previous-generation HomePod uses.) For the HomePod mini 2, the feature requires macOS 27.2. It's also supposed to work with the second-generation HomePod using the same software and the aforementioned Wi-Fi 6E requirement.

So far, new HomePod mini 2 owners are reporting two separate problems. For some, the option to enable the persistent connection never appears at all – even on hardware that meets Apple's stated requirements. For others, the connection works at first, but the Mac then falls back to its built-in or monitor speakers after sleep, a restart, or sometimes even after a single notification sound.

ran into the first problem in her review for The Verge. On a Mac mini M4 – meeting Apple's Wi-Fi 6E requirement – the persistent-output option never showed up, and the speakers behaved like ordinary AirPlay devices, along with audio artifacts, dropouts, and output switching after a restart or whenever Siri was activated on a HomePod. Tuohy said that the feature "feels unfinished," and Apple had not responded to her request for comment at the time of writing.

MacRumors forum reports. DanJoeWhitaker said they bought a stereo pair solely to use as Mac speakers, but found that the "Play sound effects through" option reverted to their Studio Display speakers within a minute, and that a single notification sound could make their Mac "forget" the HomePods entirely. 

Nismo73, tested a pair on a Mac Studio and was greeted by an error message and sound through the machine's internal speaker after the first wake from sleep. Five owners on the forums describe similar failures, and at least two forum members say they're returning the speakers. DanJoeWhitaker said they were told at an Apple Store that they weren't the first to have the problem – Apple Support's senior team reportedly offered no fix, suggesting the issue was "maybe just an early teething bug."

Redditor with an M3 Max MacBook Pro on a UniFi network. Their Mac's logs showed the point-to-point connection failing while the HomePods were on a 6GHz network, with audio falling back to standard AirPlay at around half a second of latency. Moving the speakers to a 5GHz-only network apparently restored the low-latency persistent mode in that setup. But whether the other failures correlate with 6GHz networks or specific router configurations remains unclear.

title: Apple Intelligence registered for iPad, Mac use in China
content:
Apple Intelligence won't just be available on the iPhone in China, as Apple has registered with regulators to bring it to iPad and Mac as well.


M5 MacBook Pro
After a two-year wait behind the rest of the world, the iOS 27.3 developer beta brought Apple Intelligence to China. However, while the initial introduction is on the iPhone, it won't be that way for very long.
According to the Chinese cyberspace regulator speaking to Reuters on November 9, Apple has registered for Apple Intelligence to be used on tablets and notebooks. That means it will be usable on Mac desktops, MacBooks, and iPads in the future.
